# Results (generated by `scripts/stats.py` from the committed runs and ablations)

## Headline claim

At 95% sparsity (achieved 95.00%), magnitude pruning reaches 98.15% +/- 0.11 test accuracy versus 97.97% +/- 0.15 for fisher_taylor pruning (mean +/- std over 8 seeds; dense reference 97.69% +/- 0.23). Paired difference (magnitude - fisher_taylor) +0.18 pp, 95% bootstrap CI [+0.07, +0.29], exact sign-flip p = 0.0312, magnitude better in 6/8 seeds. The 95% bootstrap CI excludes 0, so the gap is unlikely to be seed noise: magnitude is better by about 18 of 10,000 test images.

Provenance: the 95% level was named in the project plan as the claim level, but the repository cannot show that it was fixed before the sweep results existed (`CLAIM_SPARSITY` first appears in the same commit as the raw runs). It is therefore **not** described as pre-registered. The sign and size of the gap at 90% and 98% are the same (see the paired table), so the choice of level does not drive the conclusion.

## Secondary results (same sparsity)

- At 95%: fisher_taylor+regrow - fisher_taylor = +0.05 pp [-0.03, +0.11], fisher_taylor+regrow better in 6/8 seeds, p = 0.2422.
- At 95%: fisher_taylor - taylor1 = +0.29 pp [+0.19, +0.37], fisher_taylor better in 8/8 seeds, p = 0.0078.
- At 95%: taylor1 - magnitude = -0.47 pp [-0.56, -0.39], taylor1 better in 0/8 seeds, p = 0.0078.
- At 95%: fisher_taylor - fisher_taylor+oneshot = +0.56 pp [+0.46, +0.65], fisher_taylor better in 8/8 seeds, p = 0.0078.

Reading: gradient information helps only when it is the smoothed second-order term (fisher_taylor beats the single-batch first-order score and one-shot pruning), and regrowth shows no detectable effect. None of these beats plain magnitude pruning.

## Explanatory ablations

These test why magnitude wins. They do not change the headline, and nothing in them was used to choose a setting on test accuracy.

### Oracle: do the scores predict the true cost of removing a weight?

Dense seed-0 model (test acc 0.9768). Each weight is zeroed on its own and the exact validation-loss change over the full 5k validation set is measured (float64). Columns: Spearman rho against abs(dL) and against the signed dL; share of weight pairs ordered correctly by abs(dL) (all pairs / pairs on opposite sides of that criterion's own 95% threshold).

| weight set | score | rho vs abs(dL) | rho vs signed dL | pairs ok (all) | pairs ok (cross-threshold) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 500 random weights | abs(w) | +0.636 | +0.017 | 0.728 | 0.907 |
| 500 random weights | w^2 EMA[g^2] | +0.803 | +0.012 | 0.813 | 0.939 |
| 500 random weights | abs(w g) | +0.479 | +0.067 | 0.669 | 0.850 |
| 500 nearest the 95% threshold under abs(w) | abs(w) | -0.022 | -0.021 | 0.493 | 0.474 |
| 500 nearest the 95% threshold under abs(w) | w^2 EMA[g^2] | +0.504 | +0.002 | 0.679 | 0.725 |
| 500 nearest the 95% threshold under abs(w) | abs(w g) | +0.333 | -0.082 | 0.615 | 0.590 |
| 500 nearest the 95% threshold under the Fisher score | abs(w) | -0.105 | +0.033 | 0.466 | 0.436 |
| 500 nearest the 95% threshold under the Fisher score | w^2 EMA[g^2] | +0.048 | -0.079 | 0.517 | 0.505 |
| 500 nearest the 95% threshold under the Fisher score | abs(w g) | +0.200 | +0.022 | 0.568 | 0.569 |

Reading: 244 of 500 random weights *lower* validation loss when removed, so the signed change is mostly noise and no score predicts it. Against its magnitude the Fisher score tracks removal cost better than abs(w) on random weights (rho 0.80 vs 0.64). In each boundary band the selecting score has almost no spread by construction, so its own rho there is uninformative; the other score is the fairer comparison. A better single-weight predictor on the dense model is therefore not what decides the end-to-end result.

Learning rate chosen on dense validation accuracy only (seeds 100-102; 0.003: 97.28, 0.01: 97.73, 0.03: 98.09, 0.1: 97.17) -> **0.03**, then held fixed.

| method | test acc (%) | val acc (%) |
|---|---|---|
| dense | 98.18 +/- 0.08 | 98.04 +/- 0.05 |
| magnitude | 97.92 +/- 0.08 | 97.77 +/- 0.12 |
| fisher_taylor | 97.73 +/- 0.10 | 97.48 +/- 0.15 |

fisher_taylor - magnitude: -0.19 pp, 95% CI [-0.29, -0.11], sign-flip p = 0.0078, fisher_taylor better in 0/8 seeds. The gap does not depend on Adam. Under SGD the dense model beats the pruned ones, unlike under Adam.

## Cost evidence

### Cost: counted work and measured wall-clock (8 seeds' models per row)

Machine: Apple M5 (10 cores), NumPy 2.5.4, BLAS accelerate, threads 1. Speedup = median(dense x zeros) / median(path) per model; cells show the median over 8 models with the inter-quartile range. A value below 1 means slower than dense.

| method | sparsity | FLOPs / sample, CSR | FLOPs / sample, compacted | CSR b=1 | CSR b=256 | compacted b=1 | compacted b=256 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| magnitude | 90% | 9.9x fewer | 1.0x fewer | 0.24x [0.23, 0.24] | 0.013x [0.013, 0.013] | 1.02x [1.01, 1.02] | 0.84x [0.84, 0.85] |
| magnitude | 95% | 19.7x fewer | 1.0x fewer | 0.34x [0.34, 0.34] | 0.029x [0.029, 0.030] | 0.91x [0.91, 0.92] | 0.66x [0.61, 0.70] |
| magnitude | 98% | 48.2x fewer | 1.3x fewer | 0.46x [0.45, 0.46] | 0.063x [0.062, 0.063] | 1.21x [1.10, 1.23] | 0.93x [0.92, 0.94] |
| fisher_taylor | 90% | 9.9x fewer | 1.5x fewer | 0.24x [0.24, 0.24] | 0.014x [0.014, 0.014] | 1.20x [1.16, 1.23] | 0.70x [0.70, 0.72] |
| fisher_taylor | 95% | 19.7x fewer | 2.4x fewer | 0.35x [0.35, 0.35] | 0.031x [0.031, 0.032] | 1.37x [1.37, 1.38] | 1.07x [1.06, 1.12] |
| fisher_taylor | 98% | 48.2x fewer | 4.8x fewer | 0.49x [0.48, 0.49] | 0.066x [0.065, 0.067] | 1.51x [1.50, 1.51] | 1.73x [1.66, 1.81] |

Counted FLOPs and active parameters fall by the sparsity factor, but wall-clock does not follow. The CSR forward written here is slower than dense BLAS at every sparsity and batch size. Compacting away disconnected neurons and inputs helps only when pruning leaves many of them disconnected, which depends on the criterion: it speeds up fisher_taylor models from 95%, and does little or nothing (or is slower) for magnitude models. "Dense times zeros" is the reference path and is not a saving.

## Limitations

- **MNIST ceiling.** All methods land within a few tenths of a point of each other (97.7-98.3%), so the
  criteria are being separated by tens of test images out of 10,000. A harder task could separate them more
  or reverse the ordering; this one cannot say.
- **Unregularised dense baseline.** The dense model reaches 99.4% train accuracy with no regularisation. Pruned
  models beat it under Adam and lose to it under SGD, and the margin shrinks with the best-validation checkpoint.
  Read "pruned beats dense" as a statement about this baseline, not about pruning.
- **Single machine.** Wall-clock numbers come from one Apple-silicon laptop with a single BLAS thread. They show
  direction and rough size, not what a server CPU or GPU would do.
- **NumPy CSR is slower than BLAS.** The sparse-aware forward written here never beats dense BLAS. Counted FLOPs and
  active parameters fall as expected; measured latency improves only through structural compaction, and only for
  some models (see the cost table).
- **No multiple-comparison correction.** Only the 95% comparison is the headline; the other sparsity levels and
  all ablation tests are exploratory, uncorrected for the number of comparisons, and an isolated p-value near 0.05
  should not be trusted.
- **Ablations explain, they do not prove.** The oracle test uses one seed and one dense checkpoint; the SGD
  learning-rate grid is coarse; the beta sweep reports validation accuracy only.
- **fisher_taylor was changed after the first sweep** (regrowth bug and EMA bias fixed). Runs without regrowth
  reproduced bit-for-bit, so the headline numbers are unchanged; only the regrow runs were re-run.
- Eight seeds, one architecture (784-300-100-10), one dataset.
